Where Did You Buy Your License?

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Licensing Department scams - what's new, how they hook you, and when to walk away

Unique Selling Point:
Knysna's Chief Traffic Officer has invited Carte Blanche to expose corrupt licensing examiners in his department. We do a deep dive into this Western Cape Town to see who's creaming it from young drivers desperate to pass the driver's test.



Summary:
Now that the country's only driver's license card machine is back from being repaired in Germany, drivers are desperate to renew their license cards. The new online booking system is meant to streamline the process and cut out the possibility of corruption. But South African seamsters are awake and up to date. We highlight the variety of scams designed to catch motorists.
1. You arrive at Randburg License Dept at the booked timeslot, only to be told you can't enter the building because of Covid/load shedding/systems offline etc.
2. You are offered a timeslot/document/card for a fee of R250 - R1000.
3. You agree to pay and give them your ID book/card.
4. You receive your documents and pay up, only to discover later they are fake

Further information:
The long con is more elaborate and more expensive. You arrive at Florida without a timeslot and get accosted at the entrance before you enter the building.
1. You get offered a time slot for R500.
2. You give them R500 and your ID documents etc.
3. They call you to say you must pay R4000 for outstanding fines, and there are warrants of arrest on your name.
4. You pay the R4000 cash and hand it over to pay the fines.
5. They phone again to say they need R9000 to cancel the warrants of arrest. The traffic Dept will then 'refund' you the R9000. If you don't pay you face immediate arrest.
6. Two "cops" dressed in traffic uniforms come to your car to 'arrest you'.
7. You go and draw the cash and pay it to the two 'cops'.
8. They call you again to say they need another R12000. At this moment you realise this is a scam and you've lost R13500.

Script:


WHERE’D YOU BUY YOUR LICENCE?

Man: Learners or Drivers mam?

Woman: Learners.

Man: Learners for motorbike or for the normal car?

Woman: For a motorbike.

Man: I’ve got a slot for you. I can make a plan for you for now. Get your temporary license for your motorbike, go home happy today. You pay me when you’re done.

Woman: And how much is that?

Man: We’re going to charge you only R1200 for the drivers.

Woman: R1200 for the booking?

Man: For the drivers, going home with a driver’s today R1200. I’ve got someone who can help you quick-quick for R1200.

V/O: Licence Centre corruption is nothing new, but it seems to be getting worse. When South Africa’s one and only card machine went to Germany for repairs, it created a massive backlog for driving licence renewals. And while the new online booking system put a stop to endless queues, getting a time slot can be tricky. It’s a perfect storm for scammers.

Link: We all know that driving on South African roads can be dangerous but coming to a driver’s licence centre can be just as hair-raising. The minute you arrive here you’re surrounded by peddlers and anything you’re coming here for they can provide it. But do they?

V/O: Derick Cronje went to the Roodepoort Licencing Department to renew his driver’s licence because he couldn’t get a booking online. In the parking lot he was offered a time slot, for a fee.

Derick: I paid them R500. The guy took my papers. In about 10 minutes a guy phoned me. He said well Derick, we received your papers. There’s just one problem. We’ve got a few outstanding fines. So he told me it's 3200 or something. I said, Well, I'm not too sure that I owe all that money, but if he can give me the printout, I'll pay it. And he said, No, you must first pay. So I decided, okay, cool, I'll go to draw the money.

Mac: What convinced you that I need to pay these fines, were you desperate to get your licence? What was going on?

Derick: I knew I had some fines, but I wasn’t too sure what the total would have been. So I thought okay, well it is legit. I was quite desperate to get my driver’s licence, ja.

Mac: What happened after that?

Derick: And then they took the cash and gave it to the guy inside. After about 10, 15 minutes he phoned me. He said Mr Cronje we’ve processed everything, but there’s still one issue now that’s keeping up your licence. What’s the problem? He said well, you’ve got two warrants of arrest against your name, and the only way we can solve this problem is if you pay us another R9000.

Mac: Nine thousand?

Derick: R9000. So I decided, I’m like wow! I don’t have that kind of cash on me now, so you guys got to come and arrest me. And it wasn’t like 10 minutes, there were two traffic cops at my car. Said Mr Cronje, we’re here to arrest you.

Mac: When you looked at these traffic cops, they looked legit?

Derick: They were in full uniform, proper brown uniform,. Yeah, they all looked legitimate.

V/O: Intimidated by the threat of imminent arrest Derick withdrew another R9000 and handed it over. They told him to wait in the car.

Link: So imagine you’re sitting here in your car. You’ve already paid about R9000. They’ve got all your documents; they’ve got all your papers and you think they’re on the computer clearing your fines and you’re getting help. Only to find that it’s all just a scam.

Derick: About 10 minutes later they phoned me again and told me: You know what Mr Cronje? Now you need to pay us another R12000 to process all these transactions. At that stage I realised now wait, I’m busy getting a big scam

V/O: Derick was left R13500 poorer with nothing to show for it.

Mac: Do you think they’ve got people that they’re working with inside?

Derick: Definitely. Definitely, because the traffic department – I don’t know if you can get fake traffic officers inside the parking.

V/O: JMPD Spokesperson Xolani Fihla acknowledges they have a problem with scammers outside Licencing Centres.

Mac: So there might even be corrupt officers involved in these scams?

Fihla: That could be. And that’s why it’s important that if you do come across this situation, the Johannesburg Metropolitan Police Department has an internal affairs unit which monitors and investigates any misconduct, either by us or from someone outside.

V/O: But what about inside? This Learners Licence candidate was waiting to do the test for a guaranteed pass.

Journalist: Did you pay?

Man: Not now, when I’m finished here.

Journalist: How much?

Man: It’s R500.

Journalist: R500?

Man: Ja, but it’s not the same deal. It’s different here. Some they take R2000, some they take R3000.

Mac: What measures have been put into place to stop the corruption that’s happening there?

Fihla: Firstly, cameras have been installed in our stations, so supervisors are able to monitor and report any suspicious activities.

V/O: But the cameras at Florida have been turned to face the wall.

Mac: How often are these checked? I mean obviously somebody has purposely done that.

Fihla: They are checked as often as possible, but since you’ve brought that to our attention, I’ll need to take it up with the management at the Florida DLTC.

V/O: At Randburg testing centre the parking lot is no longer accessible and customers are forced to run the gauntlet of scammers down a side road. We were offered a guaranteed pass for both learners and drivers.

Journalist: Is that R2500 guaranteed pass and the booking?

Man: And the booking. The booking is R450.

Journalist: The booking is R450 for the drivers?

Man: Ja, for the drivers, and then the guaranteed pass is R2500.
So you want help on that one, or you gonna do it for yourself – for the learners? Cos you don’t have to fail, we make you pass immediately.

Journalist: You make me pass immediately?

Man: Ja, on that day. Even we can do it before that day if you want it.

Fihla: There’s no shortcuts when it comes to licencing issues. So if someone does approach you, telling you that it’s cheaper or quicker, then you should know that it’s a scam.

V/O: This motorist – let’s call him Bob – had sold his car to a dealer and urgently needed a copy of the registration papers. He applied at Randburg, but with a 4 to 6 week waiting period, he fell for a quick fix in the parking lot.

Bob: This guy approached me and said oh did you come right? Are you sorted? And I said no not at all. And then he told me he would be able to assist me, and for a fee I could get my papers within a day or two.

V/O: And voila, his document was ready the next day.

Bob: You could see the watermark on it. It certainly looked the real deal and I handed over a thousand rand and he left.

V/O: But when the dealer tried to register the car into their name they realised the document was fake.

Bob: He couldn’t see it with his naked eye, but as soon as they scanned the barcode they realised there’s nothing in this document. So it appears that they’re using their printers and in-putting information physically, but not loading it onto the system.

Mac: Would you be able to tell whether that document is real or fake?

Fihla: No, no I wouldn’t be able to tell.

Mac: To the naked eye you won’t. Because that is actually a fake document. That is a fake document.

Fihla: Because it’s got all the watermarks as well.

Mac: Do we know where they’re getting the paper from?

Fihla: Obviously these papers are issued from licencing centres. So it has to be something that's happening inside, and more stricter measures have to be taken to actually root out this corruption.

V/O: But this scourge has spread nationwide. We extended our investigation to the Southern Cape, and found that even the most picturesque of towns is not immune.

Link: Licencing corruption happens all over the country. It’s a problem that’s faced by almost every traffic department. But we came to Knysna because they asked us to step in.

V/O: For years Knysna residents have alleged that to pass their learners and drivers tests, they have to bribe the examiners. And even though the police tried to intervene, they’ve never been able to catch the culprits. But we had inside information.

Link: I don’t know about your town, but this is how it works in Knysna. The licence examiners no longer take bribes directly. They now have a middleman who gets the customers and collects all the cash on their behalf.

V/O: So we put in a call to the middleman and asked him to arrange a Learner’s Licence for a customer.

Source: Listen, man, I have someone but they want an expedited date. But I’ve got the money, it’s on me.

Magadla: When, today?

Source: Yes, today.

Magadla: Ja man. I’m hungry, man.

V/O: We arranged to meet him outside the Library with the cash, and within the hour Law Enforcement officer Thami Magadla came strolling up the road in full uniform.

Magadla: Let’s go talk over there, man.

V/O: They walked up the hill to a more secluded spot to discuss the deal and make payment.

Magadla: So, you want Code 10?

Guy: Yes

Magadla: So, go book now and get a date for Learner’s test. Very important. You get me?

Guy: Yes

Magadla: Did we discuss the money, the learners money?

Guy: Yes

Magadla: How much is it?

Guy: But I only have R1000 on me.

Magadla: What?

Source: I only have R1000 on me right now.

Magadla: No, man. Give this man R1500, man.

Source: He says it’s R1500 but I said it’s R1000.

V/O: The officer insisted that the bribe for a guaranteed pass was non-negotiable. So our informant handed over the R1000 cash with the promise of another R500 the next day. Magadla pocketed the money and then casually strolled back into town, to the Licencing Centre.
Jacobs: It’s totally unacceptable. The public should have faith in any local authority, any government institution that no corruption can take place.

V/O: Johan Jacobs is the Acting Municipal Manager of Knysna. He welcomed Carte Blanche’s intervention.

Jacobs: We’re very glad that evidence was found now and the Municipality can react to that.

Link: So we know what he looks like, we’ve seen the evidence of him taking the money. Let’s see if maybe he’ll talk to us.

V/O: We confronted Officer Thami Magadla behind the Licensing Centre.

Mac: Tat' uMagadla. How are you, sir? I'm alright, sir. My name is Macfarlane. I'm from Carte Blanche. And we want to know, sir...

Magadla: Who is this, now? What's going on here?

Mac: Why are you selling learner's licenses, Sir?

Magadla: Me?

Mac: Yup. We have you...

Magadla: No...give me... give me... no, no, no, no...

Mac: We have you accepting a bribe, tata.

Magadla: When, now?

Mac: We've got you. Who is this? Isn't this you?

Magadla: Where?

Mac: Here.

Magadla: Who is this? Yes, this is me. Who is this?

Mac: You see?

Magadla: Where?

Mac: Here's the money.

Magadla: Where? When?

Mac: At the Library Gardens. Right here. Look - that's you.

Magadla: When? Yes...When?

Mac: So, you can see what you're doing...

Magadla: No, I can see that that's me. I'm standing there. Please don't record me, man...

V/O: Once Magadla realised he couldn’t deny it, the bribe became a loan.

Magadla: No. The person at the library... you're right, I was at the library. I went to borrow money from another guy, because I was in a bind, you see.

Mac: You were going to borrow money?

V/O: But the Municipal Manager doesn’t see it that way, and they’re determined to nail the whole syndicate.

Jacobs: We will immediately start with an investigation and hopefully we will be able to connect the dots. That will make it much easier to get rid of everyone that is involved.

V/O: And they didn’t waste any time. Within the hour Officer Magadla was suspended and charges were laid at the Knysna police station.

While it may be tempting to opt for the guaranteed pass or the quick fix, it’s best to remember that all these offers are illegal and the touters and scammers are committing crime. And once you’ve been scammed there’s nobody to blame but yourself.

Bob: That piece of paper cost R1000.

Mac: It’s an expensive piece of paper.

Bob: Ja.

Mac: You must keep it and frame it.

He applied at Randburg, but with a 4 to 6 week waiting period, he fell for a quick fix in the parking lot. Bob: This guy approached me and said oh did you come right? Are you sorted? And I said no not at all. And then he told me he would be able to assist me, and for a fee I could get my papers within a day or two. V/O: And voila, his document was ready the next day. Bob: You could see the watermark on it. It certainly looked the real deal and I handed over a thousand rand and he left. V/O: But when the dealer tried to register the car into their name they realised the document was fake. Bob: He couldn’t see it with his naked eye, but as soon as they scanned the barcode they realised there’s nothing in this document. So it appears that they’re using their printers and in-putting information physically, but not loading it onto the system. Mac: Would you be able to tell whether that document is real or fake? Fihla: No, no I wouldn’t be able to tell. Mac: To the naked eye you won’t. Because that is actually a fake document. That is a fake document. Fihla: Because it’s got all the watermarks as well. Mac: Do we know where they’re getting the paper from? Fihla: Obviously these papers are issued from licencing centres. So it has to be something that's happening inside, and more stricter measures have to be taken to actually root out this corruption. V/O: But this scourge has spread nationwide. We extended our investigation to the Southern Cape, and found that even the most picturesque of towns is not immune. Link: Licencing corruption happens all over the country. It’s a problem that’s faced by almost every traffic department. But we came to Knysna because they asked us to step in. V/O: For years Knysna residents have alleged that to pass their learners and drivers tests, they have to bribe the examiners. And even though the police tried to intervene, they’ve never been able to catch the culprits. But we had inside information. Link: I don’t know about your town, but this is how it works in Knysna. The licence examiners no longer take bribes directly. They now have a middleman who gets the customers and collects all the cash on their behalf. V/O: So we put in a call to the middleman and asked him to arrange a Learner’s Licence for a customer. Source: Listen, man, I have someone but they want an expedited date. But I’ve got the money, it’s on me. Magadla: When, today? Source: Yes, today. Magadla: Ja man. I’m hungry, man. V/O: We arranged to meet him outside the Library with the cash, and within the hour Law Enforcement officer Thami Magadla came strolling up the road in full uniform. Magadla: Let’s go talk over there, man. V/O: They walked up the hill to a more secluded spot to discuss the deal and make payment. Magadla: So, you want Code 10? Guy: Yes Magadla: So, go book now and get a date for Learner’s test. Very important. You get me? Guy: Yes Magadla: Did we discuss the money, the learners money? Guy: Yes Magadla: How much is it? Guy: But I only have R1000 on me. Magadla: What? Source: I only have R1000 on me right now. Magadla: No, man. Give this man R1500, man. Source: He says it’s R1500 but I said it’s R1000. V/O: The officer insisted that the bribe for a guaranteed pass was non-negotiable. So our informant handed over the R1000 cash with the promise of another R500 the next day. Magadla pocketed the money and then casually strolled back into town, to the Licencing Centre. Jacobs: It’s totally unacceptable. The public should have faith in any local authority, any government institution that no corruption can take place. V/O: Johan Jacobs is the Acting Municipal Manager of Knysna. He welcomed Carte Blanche’s intervention. Jacobs: We’re very glad that evidence was found now and the Municipality can react to that. Link: So we know what he looks like, we’ve seen the evidence of him taking the money. Let’s see if maybe he’ll talk to us. V/O: We confronted Officer Thami Magadla behind the Licensing Centre. Mac: Tat' uMagadla. How are you, sir? I'm alright, sir. My name is Macfarlane. I'm from Carte Blanche. And we want to know, sir... Magadla: Who is this, now? What's going on here? Mac: Why are you selling learner's licenses, Sir? Magadla: Me? Mac: Yup. We have you... Magadla: No...give me... give me... no, no, no, no... Mac: We have you accepting a bribe, tata. Magadla: When, now? Mac: We've got you. Who is this? Isn't this you? Magadla: Where? Mac: Here. Magadla: Who is this? Yes, this is me. Who is this? Mac: You see? Magadla: Where? Mac: Here's the money. Magadla: Where? When? Mac: At the Library Gardens. Right here. Look - that's you. Magadla: When? Yes...When? Mac: So, you can see what you're doing... Magadla: No, I can see that that's me. I'm standing there. Please don't record me, man... V/O: Once Magadla realised he couldn’t deny it, the bribe became a loan. Magadla: No. The person at the library... you're right, I was at the library. I went to borrow money from another guy, because I was in a bind, you see. Mac: You were going to borrow money? V/O: But the Municipal Manager doesn’t see it that way, and they’re determined to nail the whole syndicate. Jacobs: We will immediately start with an investigation and hopefully we will be able to connect the dots. That will make it much easier to get rid of everyone that is involved. V/O: And they didn’t waste any time. Within the hour Officer Magadla was suspended and charges were laid at the Knysna police station. While it may be tempting to opt for the guaranteed pass or the quick fix, it’s best to remember that all these offers are illegal and the touters and scammers are committing crime. And once you’ve been scammed there’s nobody to blame but yourself. Bob: That piece of paper cost R1000. Mac: It’s an expensive piece of paper. Bob: Ja. Mac: You must keep it and frame it. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Licensing Department scams - what's new, how they hook you, and when to walk away
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Knysna's Chief Traffic Officer has invited Carte Blanche to expose corrupt licensing examiners in his department. We do a deep dive into this Western Cape Town to see who's creaming it from young drivers desperate to pass the driver's test.
metadata.Summary: Now that the country's only driver's license card machine is back from being repaired in Germany, drivers are desperate to renew their license cards. The new online booking system is meant to streamline the process and cut out the possibility of corruption. But South African seamsters are awake and up to date. We highlight the variety of scams designed to catch motorists. 1. You arrive at Randburg License Dept at the booked timeslot, only to be told you can't enter the building because of Covid/load shedding/systems offline etc. 2. You are offered a timeslot/document/card for a fee of R250 - R1000. 3. You agree to pay and give them your ID book/card. 4. You receive your documents and pay up, only to discover later they are fake
metadata.Further information: The long con is more elaborate and more expensive. You arrive at Florida without a timeslot and get accosted at the entrance before you enter the building. 1. You get offered a time slot for R500. 2. You give them R500 and your ID documents etc. 3. They call you to say you must pay R4000 for outstanding fines, and there are warrants of arrest on your name. 4. You pay the R4000 cash and hand it over to pay the fines. 5. They phone again to say they need R9000 to cancel the warrants of arrest. The traffic Dept will then 'refund' you the R9000. If you don't pay you face immediate arrest. 6. Two "cops" dressed in traffic uniforms come to your car to 'arrest you'. 7. You go and draw the cash and pay it to the two 'cops'. 8. They call you again to say they need another R12000. At this moment you realise this is a scam and you've lost R13500.
